content.question_text: According to good inheritance design, where should operations and fields that are common to multiple subclasses be placed?

core_requirements: They should be placed in the superclass.
acceptable_variations: Common fields/operations belong in the shared parent class.

content.question_text: What are the two reasons given for why you should avoid using protected fields, even though some programmers see them as a safe compromise between private and public?

core_requirements: The set of subclasses is unbounded — anyone can form a subclass and write code that directly accesses the protected field, breaking encapsulation.
In Java, all classes in the same package have access to protected fields, whether or not they are actually subclasses.
acceptable_variations: Unlimited subclass access + same-package access regardless of inheritance.

content.question_text: Unlike protected fields, what can protected methods be useful for?

core_requirements: Protected methods can indicate methods that are not ready for general use and should be redefined in subclasses.
acceptable_variations: Signaling to subclasses that a method needs to be overridden before general use.

content.question_text: In the Contractor/Employee design example, why does making Contractor a subclass of Employee violate the 'is-a' relationship?

core_requirements: A contractor is not a special case of an employee — contractors don't have a salary, are paid hourly instead, and don't stay long enough to get a raise, so the relationship fails the 'is-a' test.
acceptable_variations: Contractors and Employees differ too fundamentally (hourly pay vs salary) to be modeled as subclass/superclass.

content.question_text: In the Holiday extends GregorianCalendar example, why is it a design mistake that Holiday inherits the add method?

core_requirements: The set of holidays is not 'closed' under the inherited add operation — calling add on a holiday can turn it into a date that is no longer a holiday, meaning not all inherited methods make sense for the subclass.
acceptable_variations: Inheriting add lets you accidentally convert a Holiday into a regular, non-holiday date.

content.question_text: What does it mean to not change the expected behavior when overriding a method, and why can't the compiler enforce this for you?

core_requirements: When you override a method, you should not unreasonably change its behavior — the substitution principle applies to behavior, not just syntax.
The compiler cannot check whether your redefinition makes logical sense; it only checks that the syntax is valid.
acceptable_variations: Overriding must preserve expected behavior; the compiler only verifies syntax, not logic.

content.question_text: According to the design hints, what should you use instead of a chain of type-checking if/else statements (e.g., 'if x is of type 1... else if x is of type 2...')?

core_requirements: Use polymorphism — make the shared concept a method of a common superclass or interface, then simply call x.action() and let dynamic dispatch invoke the correct implementation.
acceptable_variations: Define a shared method in the superclass/interface and rely on dynamic binding instead of manual type checks.

content.question_text: Why does the text advise against overusing reflection in application code?

core_requirements: Reflection is fragile — the compiler cannot help find programming errors made through it, since errors are only discovered at runtime and result in exceptions.
acceptable_variations: Reflection bypasses compile-time error checking, pushing mistakes to runtime instead.
